newsitem.title: UK: Dollar takes cue from asset markets in late Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dollar takes cue from asset markets in late Europe.

text.p: The dollar rallied briefly after healthy new U.S. jobs data, but slithered from its highs in late Europe after Wall Street fell again at the opening.

March non-farm payrolls rose 175,000, below the forecast 196,000, with the February gain revised to 293,000 from 339,000. But strength shone through in a 0.4 percent rise in average hourly earnings, and a fall in the jobless rate, analysts said.

"The figures are consistent with tight labour market conditions and consistent with another rate move at the May 20 FOMC meeting," said Neil MacKinnon, chief economist at Citibank here. "I am going for another quarter point rise."

Though the dollar lost some of its shine in late dealings, it remained up on the day after an early boost from U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who calmed some fears over U.S.-Japan trade tension which have plagued the market of late.
The dollar was quoted at 1.6745/50 marks at 1513 GMT, down from its session high of 1.6795 but up from late Thursday's European level of 1.6680/90.
Dollar/yen was more resilient, trading near intraday peaks at 124.13/23, well up from Thursday's close here of 122.58/68.
Analysts said the payrolls were mildly dollar-positive, but asset market moves were swaying the currency more right now.
Graham Cocks, vice-president, treasury at Bank of Boston here, said the dollar was basically locked in familiar ranges.
"I think people's short term attitude to the dollar is completely and utterly neutral, certainly dollar/mark," he said.
Dollar/yen led the way higher overnight after the U.S. Treasury's Rubin said currencies should not be used as trade policy weapons.

During a visit to Tokyo, Rubin urged Japan not to allow its surplus to grow to a level "that is detrimental to global growth, that causes trade friction with Japan's trading partners and that could fuel protectionist sentiments".

Though Rubin's words were less incendiary than some in the market had feared, some analysts detected a veiled threat to Japan despite the assertion that the currencies should not be used to influence trade policy.
After a fairly heavy data diet this week, next week offers few U.S. figures for the market to chew on ahead of March retail sales and producer prices on Friday.

"Although there's been no sign of any inflation coming into prices so far, people will be the whole time on the lookout because failure of anything to come through on inflation will stop the Fed from tightening further," said Cocks.

The U.S. Fed funds rate rose by a quarter-point last week. Given that the Bank of Japan shows no signs of raising its rock-bottom interest rates, the yield differential should continue to support the dollar, traders said.
That, they said, made a near-term test of 125 yen likely -- though the market would become jittery of possible central bank intervention again around that key level.
Some analysts cautioned that the long wait for the next FOMC meeting meant the market should not read too much into individual data releases.
"There's a long way to go until the next meeting, so there's a lot of data to absorb before then," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered in London.
Outside the U.S., a key indicator next week will be the March German jobless data due for release on Tuesday. Unemployment rose to a post-war high in the winter.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
